Quantitative content analysis for the financing mechanisms for O&M of water infrastructure and equipment
Summary of the quantitative content analysis results of the status of water supply services of the local authorities

rationale: This mixed-methods study (structured questionnaires, key informant interviews, documentation review, narrative and quantitative content analysis, and Chi-squared cross-tabulations across 11 urban local authorities in Zimbabwe) evaluates a multi-pillar bundle of operation and maintenance (O&M) governance arrangements. Multiple rule-based mechanism families are co-equally central empirical components of the scored O&M index: (1) institutional_structure_coordination (statutory mandate allocation between ZINWA and urban councils under the ZINWA Act, Urban Councils Act, and 2012 Water Policy; central-to-local government funding policies; and municipal departmental and decentralized workshop structures, selected as primary), (2) regulatory_model_ownership (municipal department model lacking procurement/financial autonomy, ring-fencing of water accounts, absence of an independent national water regulator, and private-sector maintenance contracting), (3) fees_tariffs_subsidies (cost-recovery and earmarking rules using water tariff revenues for routine and major O&M), and (4) enforcement_sanctions (absence of legally enforceable minimum O&M/service-level standards and penalties under voluntary Service Level Benchmarking). The focal empirical outcomes—functionality of water treatment and conveyancing infrastructure, daily hours of supply continuity, and share of connected properties receiving water regularly—squarely capture effective_access (functional sustainability and service continuity/reliability).
